startup.name: Copperlane
startup.description: Copperlane sells AI agents to mortgage lenders that read an applicant's profile, verify documents and complete initial underwriting tasks, to speed up loan processing and cut errors. Lenders pay, likely per loan or per seat. Team of 3 in San Francisco, Winter 2026 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Test assumes the company was accepted, so this is only a note. Start from the roughly 1 percent prior (0.6 to 2 percent third party range). Up for a clear paying buyer and a regulated workflow with a repeatable wedge, up for AI agent timing, down because three founders with no stated mortgage background and a crowded origination automation space.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly pass because the pitch reads like many AI for mortgage applications: there is no stated lender customer, no pilot and no sign of founders who have worked inside origination. Reviewers see several same category applicants per cycle and ask what is special.

Cohorts are small.
anchors.adjustment_reason: Within 0.75 to 1.0 times the anchor. The anchor counts any seed ever, while this test asks for a round above $500K within about 12 months, which lowers it, and the 2026 AI market and a regulated workflow with a clear buyer raise it. Net near the Fintech 2022-24 anchor.

bands.rationale: Thin round, a small angel or YC follow on cheque just above the standard deal, used if lender pilots are slow.
Typical 2026 AI seed for a B2B fintech workflow tool, close to the 2022+ seed median of about $3 to 4M in the base rate tables.
Upside if two or three lenders pay in the first months and a fintech fund leads.

ladder.why_it_fails: The seed fails if lenders will not pilot a three person startup that touches borrower documents and credit decisions. Lender security reviews, vendor onboarding and fair lending checks take months, so revenue may not show in 12 months. Investors also see many AI mortgage entrants (Sei AI, Flair Labs, Kastle style companies), so a seed above $500K needs a named paying lender; Lendsnap raised little and died.

bands.rationale: Thin A after a long seed, close to the 2022+ Series A p25 of $10M but smaller.

Upside if per loan revenue scales across several mid size lenders. Sized from the 2022+ round benchmark tables for this stage, with the post money range an estimate because valuations are rarely disclosed.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A needs proof that lenders keep paying after pilots and that the agents lower cost per loan without errors. Mortgage volumes are cyclical and rate sensitive, and incumbents like Blend and the loan origination systems sell into the same buyers. Two Dots took two years to reach its A, and companies that stay at pilot stage stall like Kredi.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series B requires revenue that clearly scales beyond a few early lenders. The mortgage market has a limited number of mid size originators, long sales cycles and consolidation, and an origination system vendor could bundle similar agents. Few Fintech companies in the cohort get here and Parker shows even a large A did not guarantee a B.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series C needs a durable platform position with large lender customers and gross margins that survive model price changes. Origination automation is exposed to a regulatory shift or a housing downturn, and by that stage the market may have consolidated around the loan origination system vendors, as Blend's path suggests.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company stalls at pilot stage or is absorbed into a loan origination vendor for a small price. Lendsnap and Zinc Platform shut down in the same mortgage origination space, and Two Dots shows that only companies with real contracts get large outcomes. A billion dollar result needs the company to become the default underwriting layer, which three founders in a cyclical market are unlikely to achieve.

killers.risk: Lenders will not buy from a three person startup because of security, compliance and fair lending review
killers.evidence: Mortgage lenders run vendor risk reviews and every credit step must be auditable, which slows pilots for new vendors.
killers.mitigation: Sign one design partner lender early and pass a SOC 2 style review, keeping a human in the loop for decisions.

killers.risk: Incumbent origination platforms and LLM vendors bundle document verification and underwriting agents
killers.evidence: Blend, loan origination system vendors and general model providers already sell document understanding that lenders can switch on.
killers.mitigation: Pick a narrow high pain task like condition clearing or income calculation and prove measurable error reduction.

killers.risk: Mortgage volume stays low so lenders cut tech spend
killers.evidence: Origination volume is tied to interest rates and housing turnover, which fell sharply in 2022 to 2024.
killers.mitigation: Price per loan with savings guarantees so lenders can cut cost when volume is low.

technical_complexity.rationale: Document extraction and rules based checks are within reach of a small team using current models, but accuracy on income, assets and conditions must be near perfect and auditable. Integrations with origination systems and credit data providers are slow rather than hard.

takeover_risk.rationale: Origination platforms own the workflow and the data and can ship document and underwriting agents within a year. The startup depends on their integration access, so a platform change could cut it off.

evidence.claim: Mortgage production costs per loan have risen to many thousands of dollars, which pushes lenders to automate processing and underwriting.
Lenders and investors already buy AI document and underwriting tools in the category, showing paid demand.

roadmap.proof: One lender agreeing to a paid pilot

roadmap.goal: Raise above $500K within 12 months of the batch
actions: Run paid pilots at two or three lenders
Publish time saved per file and error reduction
roadmap.proof: Pilot revenue and a lead investor term sheet

actions: Sign a contract with a mid size lender
Integrate with the main origination systems
roadmap.proof: $1M recurring revenue and net revenue retention above 100 percent

pros.point: A regulated, paid workflow with a clear buyer
pros.evidence: Lenders already spend on processors, vendors and software for every loan, so budget exists.
Document understanding and agent models made automation of file review practical in 2025 and 2026, and two analogs raised Series A in this space.

brand.name: Copperlane
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Copperlane" --era 2022+: invented or proper noun, 10 characters, 1 word, no suffix
weaknesses: Does not say mortgage or AI
Ten characters is longer than the short names that did well in older eras
brand.rationale: Invented names are the biggest group among YC companies and show no clear gap in outcomes within eras. The name is neutral: it is easy to say and spell, and B2B lender sales depend on proof, not the name, as with Casca and Two Dots.

narrative.headline: A sensible vertical AI wedge with a paying buyer, but a crowded and cyclical mortgage market and a three person team.
narrative.general_summary: Copperlane applies AI agents to a costly, paper heavy part of mortgage lending, which is a real and paid problem. The likely path is a seed within a year if one lender pilots it, then a harder Series A that depends on repeat revenue. The main dangers are slow lender procurement, incumbents bundling the same features, and a housing cycle. The comparable companies split: Two Dots and Casca reached a Series A, while Lendsnap and Zinc Platform shut down. Estimates sit close to the Fintech cohort anchors, which rest on small samples.

assumptions: Only the input file was used for the company; market sections use general knowledge of the industry and homepage URLs, not company specific searches.
Seed in this test means a round above about $500K within 12 months of the batch start.
Cohort samples are 11 to 37 companies, so the anchors are anecdotes rather than precise rates.
